en: The attempt to KEEP the pawn — one Black player in five tries it, and the course said nothing. This is where the refutation must be known, not improvised.
We take at once, before …c6 or …e6 come to support d5. This is the only moment when that exchange wins anything.
Black is a pawn down and offers the queen trade to slow things. We accept: without queens, a pawn up is a pawn up.
The rook takes the c-file BEFORE it opens. This is the move that separates a plan from a string of natural moves.
We take the pawn back unhurried: Black could never keep it, the whole question was how many tempi it would cost us.
We hit the chain at its base. Black cannot hold everything: after the exchange, either the b5 pawn falls or the structure collapses.
The plan that creates play: we offer a pawn to open the position before Black has finished developing. The symmetry vanishes at once.
Main attack
Trap — Bg5?
White grabs e5; the Stafford reply is the surprising …Nc6.
A third of games. No capture on e5, so no Stafford: we play the Four Knights, soundly.
Nearly one game in five. Here, unlike in the gambit line, …Nxe4 is perfectly playable.
The Stafford move: offer a pawn to bring the knight back and develop at top speed.
The natural reflex — guard e4 — but it loses: …Ng4 comes and f2 collapses. Only 6.Be2! holds, and leaves White clearly better.
The natural pin… but fatal: it runs into a combination that wins the queen.
We take: the knight will drop back to c5 with tempo, and the position is sound. A Stafford player enjoys this kind of game.
Main Fianchetto
Schara-Hennig Gambit
The …c4 advance
One game in five, and the course started from 2.c4. Good news: our move doesn't change.
The Tarrasch move: …c5 challenges d4 at once, even at the cost of an isolated pawn.
The Schara-Hennig Gambit: instead of recapturing on d5, offer a pawn for rapid development.
The Rubinstein plan: Bg2 to pound the isolated d5 pawn along the long diagonal.
Push …c4: give up the isolani for queenside space.
The Tarrasch move, and it works here too: we hit d4 at once, and the bishop — gone to f4 — no longer defends b2.
White pins the defender of c5. We trade in the centre and get the active isolated pawn that is the soul of the Tarrasch.
We offer to trade White's good bishop: accept and our structure improves, retreat to g3 and a tempo is gone.
vs …e6
The Bxf6 capture
2…d5 — the classical order
A quarter of games, and the course started from …e6 or …g6. The engine suggests c4 — but that would be a Queen's Gambit, not a Torre.
The Torre move: the bishop pins f6 before e3, never shut in (unlike the Colle).
Against the fianchetto too, Bg5 pesters …Nf6 and prepares Nbd2, e3, Be2.
Trade on f6: the bishop pair versus a slight weakening of Black's structure and a coming e4 centre.
The bishop comes out, as always in the Torre. That's what makes the system playable without memorising theory.
The sharpest reply: Black hits the bishop instead of enduring the pin.
The bishop slides to f4 and stays active — trading on h4 or dropping back to e3 would abandon the idea.
Half of Black players castle here and the chapter went elsewhere. c3 supports d4 and prepares e4: the Torre plan in three moves.
We trade at the right moment: the g7 bishop loses its counterpart and the long diagonal closes on it.
2…Ne4
Pin f6 before even playing a central pawn: concrete play from move two.
Kick the bishop at once; it goes to f4 or h4.
One Black player in six fianchettoes rather than challenging the bishop. The course didn't mention it.
The aggressive line: White grabs the centre and accepts doubled pawns after …h6.
Double Black's pawns and play the structure; d5 secures a space edge.
The exchange again: Black's bishop pair offset by a clear structure and simple play.
Trade AT ONCE: this is the only moment when the exchange truly damages Black's structure, and the future g7 bishop loses its counterpart.
Recapturing with the e-pawn opens the e-file and keeps the centre; …gxf6 would wreck the coming castled position.
3…Bf5
2…e6 — the French setup
Over a quarter of games, and the course started from …d5. Black fianchettoes before committing in the centre.
A quarter of games. Black keeps …d5 in reserve and watches e4.
The Veresov move: the bishop pins f6 at once; f3 and e4 will follow to open the centre.
Black frees the bishop before …e6; White trades on f6 for the bishop pair and a half-open e-file.
Preparing e4 without allowing …Ng4: the centre will open in White's pieces' favour.
A solid setup; against …Qb6, Rb1 defends b2 and White continues Bd3, Nge2.
The system move, undistracted: the bishop pins the knight that guards d5 and e4.
We trade deliberately: without the f6 knight, e4 becomes possible and our centre takes over.
Vienna Gambit
Frankenstein-Dracula — 3.Bc4 Nxe4
2…d6 — the Philidor setup
Vienna — 3.Bc4
vs …d6
Black builds a Philidor. We can liquidate in the centre at once and trade queens on favourable terms.
The Vienna Gambit: opening the f-file for a direct attack on the king.
Quiet development… that lays a trap if Black gets greedy.
The right reaction: counterattack in the centre rather than take on f4.
Accepting is the main move — nearly four Black players in ten — and the chapter started from …d5.
The solid decline: Black props up e5 without committing. One player in five, and the course only planned for …d5 and …exf4.
Grabbing e4 unleashes the Frankenstein-Dracula: monstrous complications await.
One Black player in three simply develops instead of taking on e4 — and the course only planned for …Nxe4, the trap. You also need to know how to play when the opponent does not fall for it.
One Black player in five develops the second knight, and the course did not plan for this either.
The queen hits the e4 knight AND threatens mate on f7.
Same idea: hit e5 and open the f-file.
One Black player in five declines the gambit by propping up e5, and the course only saw the capture …exf4.
The move that justifies the gambit: the pawn kicks the knight before it settles, and the f-file will open for our rook.
Nearly six Black players in ten release the tension, and the course only saw …Nf6.
We deliberately trade queens: Black's king loses castling rights, and a slightly better endgame beats an imaginary attack.
We give up on forcing matters. The Vienna becomes a manoeuvring game where our c3 knight and c4 bishop press d5 and f7 without committing.
Black goes after our c4 bishop — the piece that gives the Vienna its bite. Worth knowing, because the plan is frequent and logical.
We recapture with the d-pawn: the d-file opens and the c4 pawn controls d5, the square the whole Vienna fights over.
The central jump to trade off our best defender of e5. We allow the trade, but recapture with the BISHOP: it lands on f3 with tempo.
We open now, before they castle: the f-file opens towards f7 and the f3 knight jumps to e5 with tempo.
We recapture with the queen: no black knight can chase her with tempo, and she will go to c4 or a4 depending on what they do.
Castling long, opposite kings: the d-file is open, our rook gets there first, and it is a race of attacks in which we lead.
